result: Nine healthy, right-handed volunteers (5 female, age 25±3 years) participated in the study.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 provide basic demographic information about the study participants. The sample size and handedness assessment are clearly stated with appropriate citation to the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory. This is standard methodological reporting.

result: The kinematic synergy model (91.1±3.6%) significantly outperformed both the individual digit model (85.9±5%) and muscle synergy model (72±7.7%) in discriminating hand postures at the behavioral level.
evaluation: Claims C3-C7 report discrimination accuracies for three models with appropriate statistical testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Bonferroni-Holm corrected). All models performed above chance (50%), with kinematic synergies showing the best performance. The statistical comparisons are properly specified.

result: The kinematic synergy model (71.58±5.52% accuracy, successful in all 9 participants) significantly outperformed both the individual digit model (63.89±6.86%, successful in 5/9 participants) and muscle synergy model (63.9±6.5%, successful in 6/8 participants) in encoding fMRI brain activity.
evaluation: Claims C8-C12 demonstrate that kinematic synergies best predict brain activity patterns. Statistical testing with appropriate corrections is reported (C11), and the kinematic model shows both higher accuracy and more consistent success across participants. The lack of difference between individual digit and muscle models (C12, p=0.95) is also properly reported.

result: Kinematic synergies accounted for 40.8% of BOLD signal variance (R²=0.41±0.06), compared to 37% for both individual digit (R²=0.37±0.03) and muscle synergy models (R²=0.37±0.06).
evaluation: Claims C13-C16 provide quantitative measures of model fit to fMRI data. The R² values show kinematic synergies explain slightly more variance than alternative models, though the difference is modest. The values are clearly reported with standard deviations.

result: The hand-posture-related network comprises bilateral precentral cortex, supplementary motor area (SMA), ventral premotor and supramarginal areas, and left inferior parietal and postcentral cortex.
evaluation: Claim C17 describes the anatomical regions identified in the group-level probability map (Figure 1). The regions are consistent with known hand motor control networks. The threshold (p>0.33, at least 4/9 subjects) is specified in C104.

result: The first three kinematic principal components explain >80% of variance and represent functionally meaningful grasping primitives: PC1 resembles power grasp (abduction-adduction and flexion-extension), PC2 represents pinch movements (thumb opposition and distal joint flexion), and PC3 represents flexion and thumb opposition.
evaluation: Claims C18-C23 characterize the kinematic synergies with quantitative variance explained and functional interpretations supported by citations to previous work (Santello et al., 1998; Gentner and Classen, 2006; Ingram et al., 2008; Thakur et al., 2008). The descriptions are consistent with established literature on hand synergies.

result: Kinematic synergies show statistically significant topographical organization in precentral and postcentral cortex (C=0.19; p=0.038), with anatomically close voxels exhibiting similar synergy coefficients.
evaluation: Claims C24-C26 report a novel topographical arrangement of synergies. While statistical significance is reported (C25), the C parameter value (0.19) is relatively low, suggesting weak topographical organization. The authors acknowledge this limitation in the discussion (C83). The finding is intriguing but requires replication and validation with larger samples or alternative methods.

result: All group correlations between fMRI and behavioral data and between behavioral models were highly significant (p<0.0001) in representational similarity analysis.
evaluation: Claim C27 reports RSA results showing significant correlations. The statistical significance is clearly stated, though the actual correlation values are referenced to supplementary materials. The high significance suggests robust relationships between neural and behavioral representations.

result: Hand postures can be decoded from fMRI activity with goodness-of-fit (R²) ranging from 0.51 to 0.90 across movements, with significant rank accuracy in 6/9 participants.
evaluation: Claims C28-C29 demonstrate successful decoding of hand postures from brain activity. The R² range shows variable but generally good reconstruction quality. Success in 6/9 participants (67%) is reasonable for this complex task, though not universal. The results support bidirectional encoding/decoding of synergies.

result: Control analyses demonstrate that kinematic synergy information in motor/premotor regions is purely motor-related, not driven by visual object presentation or visual imagery in occipital cortex.
evaluation: Claims C30-C33 report critical control analyses. Encoding with visual presentation activity failed in all participants (C30), and visual area encoding was at chance in 7/9 participants (C32). These negative controls strengthen the interpretation that synergy encoding is motor-specific, not confounded by visual processing.

result: The study employed optical motion capture (480 Hz, 26 DoF kinematic model), EMG from 5 muscles (2 kHz sampling), and 3T fMRI (TR=2.5s, TE=40ms, 1.875×1.875×3mm voxels) to record hand postures during grasping of 20 objects (5 repetitions each), with encoding analysis using leave-two-out cross-validation on 5000 initially selected voxels, retaining 1000 best-fitting voxels with cluster correction.
evaluation: Claims C90-C104 provide comprehensive methodological details. The acquisition parameters are clearly specified for all modalities. The experimental design (20 objects, 5 repetitions, randomized) and analysis pipeline (cross-validation, voxel selection, cluster correction) are well-described. The methods appear sound and appropriate for the research questions.

result: The study sample size (n=9) is comparable to previous motor control studies, and synergy results are consistent across studies using real and imagined objects with various experimental settings.
evaluation: Claims C78-C80 justify the sample size and experimental design by comparison to prior literature. Multiple citations support that n=9 is typical for this research area and that synergies are robust across different experimental conditions. This addresses potential concerns about generalizability.

result: Additional analyses with higher-dimensionality EMG or different signal processing did not improve muscle model performance, indicating limitations relate to EMG signal-to-noise ratio rather than acquisition or processing methods.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 report control analyses addressing whether muscle model underperformance was methodological. The finding that improved EMG methods don't help, consistent with prior work (Muceli et al., 2014), suggests inherent limitations of EMG for this application rather than technical shortcomings.

result: Only 40% of brain activity is explained by kinematic synergies, with remaining variance potentially related to force, non-synergistic combinations, finger enslaving, spinal coding, or other motor control aspects beyond posture.
evaluation: Claims C83-C89 acknowledge important limitations and alternative explanations. The modest variance explained (40%) is honestly reported, and multiple mechanisms that could account for remaining variance are discussed with appropriate citations. This demonstrates critical self-assessment of the model's explanatory power.

result: Hand postural information encoded through kinematic synergies is represented in cortical motor control areas, successfully discriminates grasping movements better than alternative models, can be predicted from primary motor cortex activity, supports a novel cortical organization, and has potential applications for brain-computer interfaces.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 summarize the main findings. Claims C46-C48 are well-supported by the data presented (encoding/decoding results, model comparisons). Claim C49 (novel organization) is a reasonable interpretation but somewhat overstated given the modest topographical organization (C=0.19). Claim C50 (BCI applications) is speculative but appropriately framed as potential rather than demonstrated.

result: The introduction and discussion contextualize the study within existing literature on hand motor control, synergies, somatotopy, and brain-computer interfaces, citing relevant prior work on kinematic and muscle synergies, cortical organization, and decoding methods.
evaluation: Claims C34-C77 provide background knowledge and cite prior literature appropriately. These claims establish the scientific context and justify the research questions. The citations appear relevant and accurately represented, though detailed verification of each cited claim would require consulting the original sources.

result: The width of probability maps (~1 cm on cortical mesh) corresponds to the hand area as defined by higher-resolution techniques like ultra-high field fMRI or ECoG.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 validate the spatial extent of findings by comparison to higher-resolution methods. The ~1 cm width is quantitatively stated and compared to literature (Siero et al., 2014), providing confidence that the identified regions are appropriately scaled for hand motor areas.
